content.text: On the eve of his coronation, Rama came before his father King Dasaratha and found him sitting pale and speechless, unable to look at his son. When Rama pressed his stepmother Kaikeyi to explain, she answered without shame: the king had once granted her two boons, and she now claimed them — that her own son Bharat be crowned in Rama's place, and that Rama himself go into exile in the Dandak forest for fourteen years.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: Rama's reply came without a flicker of grief: 'I, at the bidding of my sire, would cast my body to the fire, a deadly draught of poison drink, or in the waves of ocean sink: if he command, it shall be done, — my father and my king in one... It shall be done: let this suffice; Rama ne'er makes a promise twice.' He asked only why his father could not tell him this himself.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: Rama accepted the sentence outright: 'Yea, for my father's promise sake I to the wood my way will take, and dwell a lonely exile there in hermit dress with matted hair... How can I fail his will to do, friend, master, grateful sovereign too?' He asked that messengers be sent at once to recall Bharat, so the kingdom would not lack a ruler for even a day.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: When Kaikeyi, satisfied, urged him to leave the city immediately rather than wait for any formal ceremony, Rama answered with the principle that would define his life: 'I would not in this world remain a grovelling thrall to paltry gain, but duty's path would fain pursue, true as the saints themselves are true. From death itself I would not fly my father's wish to gratify... Amid all duties, Queen, I count this duty first and paramount, that sons, obedient, aye fulfil their honoured fathers' word and will.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: Rama set aside every mark of royal rank without complaint — dismissing his chariot, his men, the chouries and white umbrella used for kings — and went to comfort his mother and gather Sita before departing. The text notes that though he had just lost an empire, 'the loss of empire could not dim the glory that encompassed him,' and that no citizen who saw him pass could read any change in his bearing.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: Rama chose to conceal his own grief from the joyful crowds gathered for what they still believed was his coronation day: 'Thus to the palace Rama went where all were gay with hope and joy; but well he knew the dire event that hope would mar, that bliss destroy. So to his grief he would not yield lest the sad change their hearts might rend, and, the dread tiding unrevealed, spared from the blow each faithful friend.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

content.text: Rama's exile — accepted instantly and without bitterness to preserve his father's word — becomes the founding act of the entire epic that follows: the fourteen years in the forest, the abduction of Sita, the war in Lanka, and eventually his restoration as king. The Ramayana holds up this single moment of unhesitating obedience to a father's promise as the model of dharma placed above personal claim to power.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II
